claim: A system was developed that combines in vivo optogenetics with microdialysis and mass spectrometry-based assay to measure opioid peptide release in freely moving rodents.
source: To this end we developed a system that combines in vivo optogenetics with microdialysis and a highly sensitive mass spectrometry-based assay to measure opioid peptide release in freely moving rodents.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the development of this combined system and its application.

claim: Neuropeptides are the largest class of signaling molecules in the central nervous system.
source: Neuropeptides are the largest class of signaling molecules in the central nervous system where they act as neurotransmitters, neuromodulators, and hormones (Wotjak et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wotjak et al., 2008.

claim: Neuropeptides act as neurotransmitters, neuromodulators, and hormones.
source: Neuropeptides are the largest class of signaling molecules in the central nervous system where they act as neurotransmitters, neuromodulators, and hormones (Wotjak et al., 2008).
evidence: This functional description is supported by citation to Wotjak et al., 2008.

claim: Neuropeptides can be rapidly cleaved by peptidases.
source: In vivo neuropeptide detection is technically challenging as neuropeptides can be rapidly cleaved by peptidases and undergo posttranslational modifications.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of neuropeptides that makes detection challenging.

claim: Neuropeptides undergo posttranslational modifications.
source: In vivo neuropeptide detection is technically challenging as neuropeptides can be rapidly cleaved by peptidases and undergo posttranslational modifications.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of neuropeptides.

claim: Neuropeptides are found at orders of magnitude lower concentrations compared to classical neurotransmitters.
source: To further complicate detection, neuropeptides are found at orders of magnitude lower concentrations compared to classical neurotransmitters (i.e. glutamate, GABA, and the biogenic amines) and adsorb to a variety of surfaces during sample handling (Zhou et al., 2015; Maes et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2015 and Maes et al., 2014.

claim: Neuropeptides adsorb to a variety of surfaces during sample handling.
source: To further complicate detection, neuropeptides are found at orders of magnitude lower concentrations compared to classical neurotransmitters (i.e. glutamate, GABA, and the biogenic amines) and adsorb to a variety of surfaces during sample handling (Zhou et al., 2015; Maes et al., 2014).
evidence: This property is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2015 and Maes et al., 2014.

claim: Neuropeptides have been assayed with immunoaffinity-based techniques for decades due to their high sensitivity.
source: For decades, neuropeptides have been assayed with immunoaffinity-based techniques due to their high sensitivity (Maidment et al., 1989; Maidment et al., 1991).
evidence: This historical practice is supported by citations to Maidment et al., 1989 and 1991.

claim: Selectivity remains a concern for immunoaffinity-based techniques due to poor antibody specificity for full length vs. truncated peptides.
source: However, selectivity remains a concern due to poor antibody specificity for full length vs. truncated peptides that contain identical binding epitopes.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of immunoaffinity-based techniques.

claim: Nanoflow liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (nLC-MS) provides high sensitivity and specificity without the need for an immunocapture step.
source: Nanoflow liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (nLC-MS) is a powerful alternative for peptide detection because it provides high sensitivity and specificity without the need for an immunocapture step.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of nLC-MS over immunoaffinity-based techniques.

claim: nLC-MS has been used successfully to detect a number of endogenous peptides derived from intracranial sampling techniques such as microdialysis.
source: To this end, nLC-MS has been used successfully to detect a number of endogenous peptides derived from intracranial sampling techniques such as microdialysis (Van Wanseele et al., 2016).
evidence: This application is supported by citation to Van Wanseele et al., 2016.

claim: Opioid peptides are prominent neuromodulators for regulating motivated behaviors.
source: Opioid peptides are prominent neuromodulators for regulating motivated behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as an established role of opioid peptides.

claim: All opioid peptides except nociceptin share a common N-terminal Tyr-Gly-Gly-Phe signature sequence.
source: All opioid peptides, except nociceptin share a common N-terminal Tyr-GlyGly-Phe signature sequence, which interacts with opioid receptors.
evidence: This is stated as a structural characteristic of opioid peptides.

claim: The N-terminal Tyr-Gly-Gly-Phe signature sequence interacts with opioid receptors.
source: All opioid peptides, except nociceptin share a common N-terminal Tyr-GlyGly-Phe signature sequence, which interacts with opioid receptors.
evidence: This functional property is stated as a known characteristic.

claim: The preproenkephalin gene encodes several copies of the pentapeptide Met-enkephalin and one copy of Leu-enkephalin.
source: The preproenkephalin gene encodes several copies of the pentapeptide Met-enkephalin and one copy of Leu-enkephalin.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the preproenkephalin gene.

claim: The preprodynorphin gene encodes multiple opioid peptides, including dynorphin A, dynorphin B, and neo-endorphin.
source: The preprodynorphin gene also encodes multiple opioid peptides, including dynorphin A, dynorphin B, and neo-endorphin.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the preprodynorphin gene.

claim: The preprodynorphin-derived peptides all contain the Leu-enkephalin N-terminal sequence.
source: The preprodynorphin-derived peptides all contain the Leu-enkephalin N-terminal sequence.
evidence: This is stated as a structural characteristic of preprodynorphin-derived peptides.

claim: Enkephalins preferentially bind to the δ over μ opioid receptor.
source: To further complicate things the enkephalins preferentially bind to the δ over μ opioid receptor whereas dynorphin preferentially binds to the κ opioid receptor.
evidence: This is stated as a known binding preference of enkephalins.

claim: Dynorphin preferentially binds to the κ opioid receptor.
source: To further complicate things the enkephalins preferentially bind to the δ over μ opioid receptor whereas dynorphin preferentially binds to the κ opioid receptor.
evidence: This is stated as a known binding preference of dynorphin.

claim: Some studies have reliably detected opioid peptides in rat models.
source: Despite these complexities some studies have reliably detected opioid peptides in rat models (DiFeliceantonio et al., 2012; Mabrouk et al., 2011; Lam and Gianoulakis, 2011a; Lam and Gianoulakis, 2011b; Lam et al., 2008; Lam et al., 2010), however, it has not been previously possible to reliably detect evoked neuropeptide release in a cell-type selective manner using transgenic mouse models.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: It has not been previously possible to reliably detect evoked neuropeptide release in a cell-type selective manner using transgenic mouse models.
source: Despite these complexities some studies have reliably detected opioid peptides in rat models (DiFeliceantonio et al., 2012; Mabrouk et al., 2011; Lam and Gianoulakis, 2011a; Lam and Gianoulakis, 2011b; Lam et al., 2008; Lam et al., 2010), however, it has not been previously possible to reliably detect evoked neuropeptide release in a cell-type selective manner using transgenic mouse models.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the field prior to this work.

claim: Discrete targeting of the kappa opioid system in the nucleus accumbens can modulate both rewarding and aversive behaviors.
source: We and others have recently shown that discrete targeting of the kappa opioid system in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) can modulate both rewarding and aversive behaviors (Al-Hasani et al., 2015; Castro and Berridge, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Al-Hasani et al., 2015 and Castro and Berridge, 2014.

claim: Photostimulation of dynorphin cells in the ventral nucleus accumbens shell elicited robust aversive behavior.
source: We showed that photostimulation of dynorphin (dyn) cells in the ventral nucleus accumbens shell (vNAcSh) elicited robust aversive behavior, while photostimulation of dorsal NAcSh dyn (dNAcSh) cells induced a place preference that was positively reinforcing, however, no successful measurements of optogenetically-evoked neuropeptide release in vivo have been reported to date.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' work.

claim: Photostimulation of dorsal NAcSh dynorphin cells induced a place preference that was positively reinforcing.
source: We showed that photostimulation of dynorphin (dyn) cells in the ventral nucleus accumbens shell (vNAcSh) elicited robust aversive behavior, while photostimulation of dorsal NAcSh dyn (dNAcSh) cells induced a place preference that was positively reinforcing, however, no successful measurements of optogenetically-evoked neuropeptide release in vivo have been reported to date.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' work.

claim: No successful measurements of optogenetically-evoked neuropeptide release in vivo have been reported prior to this study.
source: We showed that photostimulation of dynorphin (dyn) cells in the ventral nucleus accumbens shell (vNAcSh) elicited robust aversive behavior, while photostimulation of dorsal NAcSh dyn (dNAcSh) cells induced a place preference that was positively reinforcing, however, no successful measurements of optogenetically-evoked neuropeptide release in vivo have been reported to date.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the field that this study addresses.

claim: Few reports have extensively investigated regional distinctions within the NAc shell.
source: Furthermore, few reports have extensively investigated regional distinctions within the NAc shell and no reports to our knowledge have successfully measured optogenetically-evoked neuropeptide release in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: A custom optogenetic-microdialysis probe was developed that simultaneously provides photostimulation with the ability to sample local neurochemical release in awake, freely moving mice.
source: We developed a custom optogenetic-microdialysis (opto-dialysis) probe that simultaneously provides photostimulation with the ability to sample local neurochemical release in awake, freely moving mice.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological development in the study.

claim: A targeted nLC-MS method was established to analyze dynorphin, leu-enkephalin, met-enkephalin, dopamine, GABA and glutamate.
source: We established a targeted nLC-MS method to analyze the opioid peptides dyn (fragment dynorphin A1-8) and enkephalins (leu- and met-), as well as dopamine, GABA and glutamate.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological development in the study.

claim: Isotopically labeled dynorphin (DYN*) with 13C615N1-leucine was used as an internal standard with a mass shift of +7 and a +3.5 m/z shift.
source: To establish a quantitative assay, we used a custom synthesized isotopically labeled dyn (DYN*, YGGFLRRI with isotope 13C615N1-leucine) with a mass shift of +7 and a +3.5 m/z shift (+2 charge state) as an internal standard (IS) to account for variability during the LC injection, surface adsorption, and ionization efficiency.
evidence: This is described as part of the experimental method.

claim: High concentration injections of DYN* were fully resolved by the mass spectrometer and did not result in cross talk with endogenous dynorphin.
source: High concentration injections of DYN* were fully resolved by the mass spectrometer and did not result in cross talk with endogenous dyn (Figure 1a and b), demonstrating that the addition of labeled DYN* does not contribute to or interfere with the endogenous dyn signal, while maintaining a similar retention time.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1a and b.

claim: The addition of labeled DYN* does not contribute to or interfere with the endogenous dynorphin signal.
source: High concentration injections of DYN* were fully resolved by the mass spectrometer and did not result in cross talk with endogenous dyn (Figure 1a and b), demonstrating that the addition of labeled DYN* does not contribute to or interfere with the endogenous dyn signal, while maintaining a similar retention time.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 1a and b.

claim: All three opioid peptides (dynorphin, Leu-Enkephalin, Met-Enkephalin) and isotopically labeled DYN* were detected within 5 min following loading and desalting the sample on the column.
source: To further validate the use of DYN* as an internal standard when detecting opioid peptides we prepared a linear calibration curve with a mixture of dyn, Leu-Enkephalin (LE) and Met-Enkephalin (ME) standards spiked with DYN* and detected all four compounds within 5 min following loading and desalting the sample on the column.
evidence: This is stated as a validation result for the method.

claim: Four distinct peaks are shown in the reconstructed ion chromatographic trace, confirming the separation and reliable detection of all three opioid peptides with isotopically labeled DYN* in one sample.
source: Four distinct peaks are shown in the reconstructed ion chromatographic trace, confirming the separation and reliable detection of all three opioid peptides with isotopically labeled DYN* in one sample (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the chromatogram shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The addition of the DYN* isotope improves quantification by improving relative standard deviation for repeated injections of standards.
source: The addition of the DYN* isotope to our assay further improves quantification by improving relative standard deviation for repeated injections of standards (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1d-f.

claim: No effect of dialysate matrix for any targeted analyte was observed.
source: No effect of dialysate matrix for any targeted analyte was observed (Figure 1g–j).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 1g-j.

claim: The opto-dialysis probe has a maximal diameter of 480 μm.
source: This resulted in a maximal probe diameter of 480 μm.
evidence: This is stated as a specification of the probe design.

claim: A 60 kDa molecular weight cutoff, polyacrylonitrile membrane with a slight negative charge was used for optimal peptide recovery.
source: To maximize concentrations of peptides entering the probe, we used a 60 kDa molecular weight cutoff, polyacrylonitrile membrane with a slight negative charge for optimal peptide recovery (AN69, Hospal, Bologna Italy) (Zhou et al., 2015; Maidment et al., 1989) and showed we can measure changes in peptide stock concentration within the 15 min fraction collection time (Figure 2b).
evidence: This design choice is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2015 and Maidment et al., 1989.

claim: Changes in peptide stock concentration can be measured within the 15 min fraction collection time.
source: To maximize concentrations of peptides entering the probe, we used a 60 kDa molecular weight cutoff, polyacrylonitrile membrane with a slight negative charge for optimal peptide recovery (AN69, Hospal, Bologna Italy) (Zhou et al., 2015; Maidment et al., 1989) and showed we can measure changes in peptide stock concentration within the 15 min fraction collection time (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: AAV5-EF1α-DIO-ChR2-eYFP was injected into either the vNAcSh or the dNAcSh of preprodynorphin-IRES-cre mice.
source: To evoke and measure in vivo peptide release we injected AAV5-EF1α-DIO-ChR2-eYFP in to either the vNAcSh or the dNAcSh of preprodynorphin-IRES-cre (dyn-cre) mice and implanted the custom opto-dialysis probes 3 weeks later (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is described as part of the experimental procedure and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Custom opto-dialysis probes were implanted 3 weeks after viral injection.
source: To evoke and measure in vivo peptide release we injected AAV5-EF1α-DIO-ChR2-eYFP in to either the vNAcSh or the dNAcSh of preprodynorphin-IRES-cre (dyn-cre) mice and implanted the custom opto-dialysis probes 3 weeks later (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is described as part of the experimental timeline shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Artificial cerebrospinal fluid was perfused through the device at 0.8 μL/min.
source: Following recovery artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF) was perfused through the device at 0.8 μL/min and fractions were collected on ice every 15 min, generating 12 μL volumes, 2 μL of which were aliquoted and used for a small molecule detection assay.
evidence: This is described as part of the experimental procedure.

claim: Fractions were collected on ice every 15 min, generating 12 μL volumes.
source: Following recovery artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF) was perfused through the device at 0.8 μL/min and fractions were collected on ice every 15 min, generating 12 μL volumes, 2 μL of which were aliquoted and used for a small molecule detection assay.
evidence: This is described as part of the experimental procedure.

claim: Three baseline fractions were collected prior to photostimulation.
source: Three baseline fractions were collected prior to a fraction capturing 15 min of 10 Hz (10 ms pulse width) photostimulation, and six additional fractions were collected following photostimulation.
evidence: This is described as part of the experimental procedure.

claim: Photostimulation was delivered at 10 Hz with 10 ms pulse width for 15 min.
source: Three baseline fractions were collected prior to a fraction capturing 15 min of 10 Hz (10 ms pulse width) photostimulation, and six additional fractions were collected following photostimulation.
evidence: This is described as part of the experimental procedure.

claim: Six additional fractions were collected following photostimulation.
source: Three baseline fractions were collected prior to a fraction capturing 15 min of 10 Hz (10 ms pulse width) photostimulation, and six additional fractions were collected following photostimulation.
evidence: This is described as part of the experimental procedure.

claim: 100 mM K+ aCSF was infused at the end of each collection experiment as a positive control.
source: As a positive control for detecting dynamic changes in vivo by nLC-MS and to establish sampled neuron responsivity to stimuli, we infused 100 mM K+ aCSF at the end of each collection experiment.
evidence: This is described as part of the experimental procedure.

claim: The influx of K+ ions causes depolarization, resulting in vesicular exocytosis, which is expected to evoke a large increase in peptide concentration.
source: The influx of K+ ions causes depolarization, resulting in vesicular exocytosis, which is expected to evoke a large increase in peptide concentration.
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for using K+ as a positive control.

claim: Mice were included in the study if 100 mM K+ stimulation resulted in a positive increase in analytes at the end of the experiment.
source: Mice were included in the study if 100 mM K+ stimulation resulted in a positive increase in analytes at the end of the experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–c) and if correct anatomical probe placement and viral expression were confirmed (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a and b).
evidence: This is stated as an inclusion criterion for the study.

claim: Mice were included in the study if correct anatomical probe placement and viral expression were confirmed.
source: Mice were included in the study if 100 mM K+ stimulation resulted in a positive increase in analytes at the end of the experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–c) and if correct anatomical probe placement and viral expression were confirmed (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a and b).
evidence: This is stated as an inclusion criterion for the study.

claim: 81.1% (15/18) of the mice were included in the analysis.
source: In the current study 81.1% (15/18) of the mice were included in the analysis.
evidence: This is stated as the success rate for the study.

claim: A significant increase in dynorphin was detected in dyn-cre positive mice during photostimulation in the vNAcSh compared to control mice.
source: A significant increase in dyn was detected in dyn-cre positive mice during photostimulation in both the vNAcSh (interaction effect; t = 3.941, p<0.001) and dNAcSh (interaction effect; t = 3.012, p=0.003), compared to control mice (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: A significant increase in dynorphin was detected in dyn-cre positive mice during photostimulation in the dNAcSh compared to control mice.
source: A significant increase in dyn was detected in dyn-cre positive mice during photostimulation in both the vNAcSh (interaction effect; t = 3.941, p<0.001) and dNAcSh (interaction effect; t = 3.012, p=0.003), compared to control mice (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In the vNAcSh there was a sustained increase in dynorphin after photostimulation.
source: Interestingly, in the vNAcSh there was also a sustained increase in dyn after photostimulation (interaction effect; t = 2.499, p=0.014) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Dynorphin release during photostimulation was significantly higher in the vNAcSh compared to the dNAcSh.
source: Dyn release during photostimulation was also significantly higher in the vNAcSh compared to the dNAcSh (interaction effect; t = 2.749, p=0.007) and post stimulation (interaction effect; t = 2.806, p=0.006) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Dynorphin release post stimulation was significantly higher in the vNAcSh compared to the dNAcSh.
source: Dyn release during photostimulation was also significantly higher in the vNAcSh compared to the dNAcSh (interaction effect; t = 2.749, p=0.007) and post stimulation (interaction effect; t = 2.806, p=0.006) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Photostimulation of vNAcSh dynorphin neurons was previously shown to cause aversive behavior.
source: Photostimulation of vNAcSh dyn neurons was previously shown to cause aversive behavior, consistent with early pharmacological studies which linked dyn with negative emotional states (Al-Hasani et al., 2015; Bals-Kubik et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Al-Hasani et al., 2015 and Bals-Kubik et al., 1993.

claim: Early pharmacological studies linked dynorphin with negative emotional states.
source: Photostimulation of vNAcSh dyn neurons was previously shown to cause aversive behavior, consistent with early pharmacological studies which linked dyn with negative emotional states (Al-Hasani et al., 2015; Bals-Kubik et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bals-Kubik et al., 1993.

claim: During photostimulation of dyn-containing cells in the dNAcSh, Leu-Enkephalin levels were significantly elevated compared to controls.
source: During photostimulation of dyn-containing cells in the dNAcSh, LE levels were significantly elevated compared to controls (interaction effect; t = 5.384, p<0.0001) (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: No changes in Leu-Enkephalin were detected during photostimulation of dyn-containing cells in the vNAcSh.
source: In contrast, no changes in LE were detected during photostimulation of dyn-containing cells in the vNAcSh (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: A significant increase in Met-Enkephalin was observed during photostimulation of dyn-containing cells in the vNAcSh.
source: Converse to this, we observed a significant increase in ME during photostimulation of dyn-containing cells in the vNAcSh (comparing cre + and cre-, interaction effect; t = 2.824, p=0.006).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The same effect on Met-Enkephalin was not significant in the dNAcSh when comparing cre+ and cre- mice.
source: However, the same effect was not significant in the dNAcSh (comparing cre + and cre-, t = 1.78, p=0.053) (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3d.

claim: A significant change in Met-Enkephalin was observed in the dNAcSh when compared to its baseline.
source: Importantly, we observed a significant change in ME in the dNAcSh when compared to its baseline (t = 1.94, p=0.033), and there was no significant difference between the effect of photostimulation in ventral and dorsal (i.e. both are increased).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference between the effect of photostimulation on Met-Enkephalin in ventral and dorsal NAcSh.
source: Importantly, we observed a significant change in ME in the dNAcSh when compared to its baseline (t = 1.94, p=0.033), and there was no significant difference between the effect of photostimulation in ventral and dorsal (i.e. both are increased).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Baseline levels of opioid peptides in dNAcSh are higher than the vNAcSh (7.114 pM versus 2.71 pM, respectively).
source: However, the lack of a significance between Cre + and Cre- in dNAcSh is likely due, at least in part, to the fact the baseline levels of opioid peptides in dNAcSh are higher than the vNAcSh (7.114 pM versus 2.71 pM, respectively).
evidence: This is stated as a measured difference in baseline levels.

claim: The range of absolute dialysate concentration detected for dynorphin was 0.28–0.44 pM in dNAcSh and 0.13–0.28 pM in vNAcSh.
source: Though data are represented as % of baseline the range of absolute dialysate concentration detected for dyn was 0.28–0.44 pM in dNAcSh and 0.13–0.28 pM in vNAcSh; LE 1.39–3.28 pM in dNAcSh and 1.30–2.24 pM in vNAcSh; ME 6.19–8.69 pM in dNAcSh and 2.57–4.11 pM.
evidence: This is stated as the measured concentration range.

claim: The range of absolute dialysate concentration detected for Leu-Enkephalin was 1.39–3.28 pM in dNAcSh and 1.30–2.24 pM in vNAcSh.
source: Though data are represented as % of baseline the range of absolute dialysate concentration detected for dyn was 0.28–0.44 pM in dNAcSh and 0.13–0.28 pM in vNAcSh; LE 1.39–3.28 pM in dNAcSh and 1.30–2.24 pM in vNAcSh; ME 6.19–8.69 pM in dNAcSh and 2.57–4.11 pM.
evidence: This is stated as the measured concentration range.

claim: The range of absolute dialysate concentration detected for Met-Enkephalin was 6.19–8.69 pM in dNAcSh and 2.57–4.11 pM in vNAcSh.
source: Though data are represented as % of baseline the range of absolute dialysate concentration detected for dyn was 0.28–0.44 pM in dNAcSh and 0.13–0.28 pM in vNAcSh; LE 1.39–3.28 pM in dNAcSh and 1.30–2.24 pM in vNAcSh; ME 6.19–8.69 pM in dNAcSh and 2.57–4.11 pM.
evidence: This is stated as the measured concentration range.

claim: A benzoyl chloride (BzCl) derivatization LC-MS method was applied to monitor dopamine, GABA and glutamate in dialysis samples.
source: To determine if peptide release corresponded with small molecule neurotransmitter release, we applied a benzoyl chloride (BzCl) derivatization LC-MS method to monitor three small molecules, dopamine, GABA and glutamate in dialysis samples (Song et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is described as part of the experimental method and supported by citations.

claim: Dopamine increased in the dNAcSh during photostimulation.
source: Interestingly, dopamine increased in the dNAcSh during photostimulation (interaction effect; t = 5.007, p<0.0001), which persisted following stimulation (interaction effect; t = 2.081, p=0.039) (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Dopamine increase in the dNAcSh persisted following stimulation.
source: Interestingly, dopamine increased in the dNAcSh during photostimulation (interaction effect; t = 5.007, p<0.0001), which persisted following stimulation (interaction effect; t = 2.081, p=0.039) (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Levels of GABA increased in the vNAcSh following photostimulation and had a prolonged response.
source: Levels of GABA also increased in the vNAcSh following photostimulation (t = 2.363, p=0.020) and had a prolonged response (t = 4.744, p<0.0001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a.

claim: There were no significant changes in glutamate levels during photostimulation in either vNAcSh or dNAcSh.
source: There were no significant changes in glutamate levels during photostimulation in either vNAcSh or dNAcSh (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Photostimulation of dyn-containing cells in the vNAcSh and dNAcSh results in a detectable increase in dynorphin release, which is greater in the vNAcSh.
source: The data show that photostimulation of dyn-containing cells in the vNAcSh and dNAcSh results in a detectable increase in dyn release, which is greater in the vNAcSh.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the results.

claim: The result correlates with previous behavioral data demonstrating that dynorphin release likely drives a region dependent preference and aversion behavior.
source: This result correlates with previous behavioral data demonstrating that dyn release likely drives a region dependent preference and aversion behavior (Al-Hasani et al., 2015).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citation to Al-Hasani et al., 2015.

claim: The preference behavior when photostimulating dynorphin cells in the dNAcSh may be related to the detected increases in dopamine and Leu-Enkephalin.
source: Importantly, we previously observed a preference behavior when photostimulating dyn cells in the dNAcSh and these data suggest that the preference may be related, at least in part, to the detected increases in dopamine and LE.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: Many studies have shown that levels of both dopamine and Leu-Enkephalin increase during preference or reward.
source: Furthermore, many studies have shown that levels of both dopamine and LE increase during preference or reward (Olds, 1982; Spanagel et al., 1990; Bruijnzeel, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Olds, 1982; Spanagel et al., 1990; and Bruijnzeel, 2009.

claim: Using this method it is not possible to know whether Leu-Enkephalin is derived from preprodynorphin or preproenkephalin.
source: Importantly, using this method it is not possible to know whether LE is derived from pDyn or pENK but in future experiments we can combine this with conditional knockout approaches to selectively delete the peptides in specific cell types, so that we can later determine what happens to these signals in the absence of expression of particular peptides in D1 vs D2 cells and subregions.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current method.

claim: Optogenetic activation of D1 cells could impart changes on D2 cell activity thereby releasing Met-Enkephalin indirectly.
source: In addition, we cannot preclude interactions between MSN cell types, specifically that optogenetic activation of D1 cells could impart changes on D2 cell activity thereby releasing Met-Enk, indirectly, and/or via indirect circuits outside the NAc.
evidence: This is stated as a possible alternative explanation.

claim: Dopamine release via D1 MSN stimulation could be via indirect suppression of D1 projections back to VTA GABA neurons.
source: In addition, dopamine release via D1 MSN stimulation, could be via two mechanisms 1) via indirect suppression of D1 projections back to VTA GABA neurons (Edwards et al., 2017), which acts via GABA-B to disinhibit VTA DA neurons.
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Edwards et al., 2017.

claim: Indirect suppression of D1 projections to VTA GABA neurons acts via GABA-B to disinhibit VTA dopamine neurons, resulting in dopamine release in the NAc.
source: In addition, dopamine release via D1 MSN stimulation, could be via two mechanisms 1) via indirect suppression of D1 projections back to VTA GABA neurons (Edwards et al., 2017), which acts via GABA-B to disinhibit VTA DA neurons. This would then result in dopamine release in the NAc following D1 stimulation.
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Edwards et al., 2017.
